lesson.title: Taking Control: How Experiments Manufacture Evidence for Cause and Effect
lesson.summary: An experiment is a study in which researchers deliberately impose treatments on the units being studied, which is what allows a well-designed experiment, unlike an observational study, to support a genuine claim of causation.
lesson.body:
An experiment is a study in which the researcher deliberately imposes one or more treatments on the units being studied and then measures the response, rather than simply observing conditions that already exist. This active manipulation is what separates an experiment from an observational study, and it is the reason experiments occupy a special place in statistics: they are the study design best suited to supporting a genuine claim of causation.

Causation is difficult to establish from data you merely observe, because any relationship you notice might be driven by a lurking variable rather than by one variable truly causing the other, exactly the trap illustrated by Simpson's paradox, where a confounding variable unevenly spread across groups can flip or fabricate an apparent trend. If students who use a certain study app also happen to be more motivated to begin with, comparing app users to non-users will always be contaminated by motivation, no matter how large the sample. An experiment attacks this problem directly by controlling who receives which treatment. When researchers assign treatments themselves, ideally at random, they can balance lurking variables across treatment groups so treatment becomes the only systematic difference left, which is what allows a resulting difference in outcomes to be attributed to the treatment rather than to some hidden third factor.

Suppose agricultural researchers want to know whether a new fertilizer increases corn yield. In an observational study, they might record yields on farms that already happen to use the fertilizer versus farms that do not, but farms differ in soil quality, rainfall, and farmer skill, so any yield difference is tangled up with those factors. In an experiment, the researchers instead take 40 identical plots of land, randomly assign the new fertilizer to 20 of them and a standard fertilizer to the other 20, hold watering, sunlight, and planting density constant across all 40 plots, and measure yield at harvest. Suppose the new-fertilizer plots average 178 bushels per acre and the standard-fertilizer plots average 164 bushels per acre. Because random assignment should have balanced soil quality and other lurking variables evenly across the two groups of plots, the 14 bushel per acre gap can reasonably be attributed to the fertilizer itself.

Every experiment shares a common vocabulary that the rest of this unit unpacks piece by piece: the units that receive a treatment, the treatment itself, the factor or factors being varied, and the control group used for comparison. Getting these pieces right is what turns a study into a genuine experiment rather than a glorified observation with extra steps.

Experiments are powerful, but they are not always possible or ethical. Researchers cannot randomly assign people to smoke for thirty years or randomly assign countries to different economic policies, so many important questions can only be studied observationally, which is precisely why comparing the strengths and limitations of experiments against observational studies, the subject of the next section, matters so much in practice.
